text: In Germany, Poland, and their diaspora, it is common for Germans and Poles to engage in cross-cultural interactions, encompassing visits, dating, and even military aid, with the goal of building relationships, assimilating, and acknowledging cultural similarities. This behavior is typically observed within the contexts of friendship, family, and neighborly relations. Both groups reciprocate acceptance and active participation in these cross-cultural interactions, reflecting a mutual openness to cultural exchange. The dynamics of these interactions are influenced by factors such as migration, language retention, and historical context, shaping the nature of the relationships between the two cultural groups. While not universally prevalent, a significant portion of the sampled population regards these cross-cultural interactions as a relatively common and accepted practice within the German and Polish cultural contexts.

In both historical and contemporary Poland, Polish people and society actively embrace and uphold their cultural identity while also promoting peaceful coexistence and engaging in cultural exchange with various groups, including minorities, immigrants, and other cultures. The goal behind this behavior is to preserve their cultural identity, maintain harmony, and gain exposure to different cultural experiences. This approach is influenced by Poland's diverse cultural history and its evolution into a multicultural nation. The sampled population widely regards this behavior as normative, reflecting a strong acceptance of cultural diversity and peaceful coexistence within Polish society.

In Poland and Polish culture, various artists, including Dawid Podsiadlo, Zakopower, Maryla Rodowicz, Żywiołak, DOKTÓR HAŁABAŁA i SIEDMIU ZBÓJÓW, and Daria Zawiałow, engage in creating, performing, and enjoying a diverse range of music, spanning from folk to rock, which includes remakes and new interpretations of classic songs. This musical expression serves the goals of entertainment, cultural preservation, and sharing Polish culture with others. Audiences actively participate by listening, enjoying, and celebrating this musical heritage, which also includes references to TV series and movies, and spans over 60 years of music history. This vibrant music scene is widely regarded as a normative and integral part of Polish cultural identity by a significant portion of the sampled population.

In Poland and Polish communities globally, various actors including children, parents, and equivalents of Santa Claus engage in celebratory activities and gift-giving on occasions such as Dzień Matki, Mikołaj, and Gwiazdka, each with distinct dates and gift-giving practices. The goal of these behaviors is to celebrate and honor, with children and mothers being the recipients of these gifts and celebrations. This celebratory and gift-giving tradition is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population, with a significant portion agreeing that it is a standard way of expressing love and appreciation within Polish culture.

In Polish naming practices and conventions, it is customary for Polish people and parents to use diminutive names, traditional and historical names, and the -ski or -ska suffix for surnames as a way to express affection, identify nationalities, and denote origin or association with a specific town. This naming tradition serves the goal of naming newborns and expressing affection, while also reinforcing the parent-child and self-reference relationships. The names chosen are not considered exotic or foreign, but rather old-fashioned or universal European names, with names ending in -sław(a) being perceived as old-fashioned. This naming convention is widely regarded as the norm within the sampled population, reflecting a high level of adherence to these traditional practices.

In various settings in Poland, including rural areas, cities, suburbs, and post-socialist Poland, Polish people, encompassing adults, students, and the working class, engage in a wide range of behaviors such as migrating, living with parents, moving to large cities and suburbs, and even resorting to theft for survival and financial stability. These actions are driven by a history of poverty, internal migration, and a transition from an unemployment crisis to growth. The Polish society, parents, and residential areas play a role in supporting, growing, and adapting to these changes. This behavior is considered relatively normative within the sampled population, reflecting the complex dynamics of survival, adaptation, and socio-economic shifts within Polish society.

In Poland and Polish-speaking communities, Polish artists, filmmakers, and audiences actively engage in creating, writing, watching, and appreciating Polish literature and films. This cultural exchange forms a significant part of Polish identity, with a strong emphasis on Polish culture, history, and identity, including themes related to WWII, Poland, and Russia. The goal of this behavior is to express, entertain, enlighten, and enjoy, fostering a deep connection to their cultural heritage. The creation and consumption of Polish literature and films are widely regarded as a normative and integral part of the cultural fabric by a significant portion of the sampled population, reflecting the strong influence and appreciation for their artistic expressions.

In various contexts, including interactions within Poland and with foreigners, Polish speakers and learners actively engage in learning and using the Polish language, with a specific focus on pronunciation and dialects. Their goal is to connect, communicate effectively, and perfect their pronunciation. This emphasis on pronunciation includes mastering unique letter combinations and regional dialects. When engaging in communication, both other Polish speakers and foreigners respond, listen, and actively participate. This behavior is widely regarded as a standard practice within the Polish cultural group, with a significant portion of the sampled population valuing the importance of language learning and pronunciation in connecting with others.

In Polish folklore, cultural products, and The Witcher series, there is a noticeable effort by people of color and Polish actors to advocate for diversity and inclusion in cultural representation and casting. Their goal is to promote diversity and accurately represent Polish culture by seeking more inclusive and diverse portrayals. This behavior has led to the inclusion of people of color and Polish actors in major roles, reflecting a historical basis while not strictly adhering to historical accuracy and incorporating elements from other cultures. While not universally embraced, this push for diversity and inclusion is recognized by a significant portion of the sampled population within the Polish cultural context.

In various settings such as everyday life, school exchanges, and personal and professional relationships, Polish individuals and groups are commonly observed expressing frustration, communicating effectively, maintaining cleanliness, and behaving in a friendly and helpful manner. This behavior extends to interactions with non-Polish individuals, where positive social interactions and fulfilling work responsibilities are prioritized. Recipients, including Polish people, partners, and non-Polish individuals, respond by laughing, expressing surprise, collaborating, interacting positively, and listening attentively. It is noteworthy that encountering an unenjoyable Polish person is a rarity. This pattern of behavior is widely regarded as normative within the sampled population, indicating a high level of acceptance and prevalence within Polish culture across various relationships and environments.

In the context of Polish language usage, Polish speakers commonly incorporate specific words and phrases, including loanwords, to describe various objects and concepts when communicating with listeners or devices. The goal of this behavior is to effectively communicate and describe different elements. However, there is a perception within the culture that certain words may be inappropriate or too similar to their English equivalents. This practice of using loanwords and specific phrases is perceived as moderately common within the sampled population, with around half of the population engaging in this behavior. This suggests that there is a balanced perspective on the normativity of this linguistic practice among Polish speakers.

In Polish radio stations, both the Polish people and the stations themselves engage in the behavior of playing music that caters to specific musical preferences and broadcasting religious content, with the goal of entertaining and providing religious services to their listeners. The music played on these stations varies from pop, soft rock, and oldies to religious music, reflecting the diverse tastes and religious inclinations of the audience. This practice is widely regarded as a standard and common approach within the sampled population, indicating that a significant portion of the population finds this behavior normative.

In Poland and Polish communities abroad, both individuals and shopkeepers actively participate in the buying and selling of secondhand items, including traditional food products like gherkins and pickles. This behavior serves the dual purpose of obtaining used items at a lower cost and meeting the needs of customers seeking affordable goods. Customers, in turn, engage in the cultural tradition of purchasing secondhand items and embracing the consumption of traditional Polish foods, such as pickles. Notably, pickles hold a significant place in Polish culinary heritage, with British Lipton being the most popular brand. This practice is widely regarded as a normative and standard behavior within the sampled population, reflecting a strong cultural affinity for thriftiness and the preservation of culinary customs.

In various settings including Poland, the University of Toronto, and global interactions, Polish people and their descendants actively engage in self-identification, cultural preservation, and expressing their heritage. Their goal is to acknowledge, preserve, and express their Polish identity, which is reciprocated by others who acknowledge and provide platforms for recognition. There is an emphasis on cultural differences and sub-ethnicities within this behavior, reflecting the diverse and multifaceted nature of Polish identity. This behavior is widely regarded as normative among a significant portion of the sampled population, indicating a strong commitment to preserving and celebrating Polish culture and heritage.

In various settings such as weddings, special occasions, and modern Poland, it is customary for people of all ages, including children and adults, to don traditional clothing and engage in traditional dances like the Polonez. This behavior serves the purpose of preserving and representing Polish culture, with the goal of both upholding tradition and deriving enjoyment from the festivities. The social and cultural relation between individuals is strengthened as they actively participate in these traditions, fostering a sense of shared identity and heritage. However, it is worth noting that the tradition of wearing traditional clothing, which has three variants, is gradually declining. Despite this, a significant portion of the sampled population still regards these cultural practices as a meaningful and normative part of Polish social life.

In the context of game development and folklore representation within the Polish cultural group, Polish game developers and folklore creators prioritize the creation of games and folklore that authentically reflect Polish heritage, often without incorporating racial diversity. Their goal is to preserve their cultural heritage and offer genuine representations. However, this approach has been met with criticism from players and the global market for its lack of racial diversity, which has been interpreted by some as racism. This behavior is considered controversial and is not widely regarded as normative within the sampled population.

In the context of marriage and identity within the Polish cultural group, it is common for wives to retain or combine their last names, often preferring to keep their original surname. This practice aims to maintain or merge individual identities within the marital union. Notably, Polish names can be lengthy, and approximately 85% of Polish wives choose to keep their last name, reflecting a strong preference for this tradition. This behavior is widely regarded as the norm within the sampled population, indicating a high level of acceptance and prevalence among the Polish cultural group.

In Polish primary and secondary education, schools, students, and teachers place a strong emphasis on preserving and celebrating Polish language, culture, and identity. This is achieved through the study of literature, history, and the observance of national holidays. The goal is to instill a deep appreciation for Polish heritage and language among the students. As part of the educational and social relationship, students and peers actively participate in cultural activities and engage in learning Polish literature. The educational system includes unregulated niche schools and incorporates compulsory reading, as well as learning patriotic rhymes and songs to reinforce the importance of Polish identity. This cultural practice is widely regarded as the standard within the sampled population, reflecting a high level of normativity.

In Poland and European settings, people from the Polish cultural group are known for their preference for and preparation of meat-based dishes, particularly pork, meatballs, and spaghetti. This culinary inclination is accompanied by a strong emphasis on promoting their food culture, aiming to satisfy hunger and potentially win a "cultural war" through their gastronomic offerings. Additionally, maize porridge, known as "mamałga," holds significance as a common food item within this cultural context. The consumption and preparation of meat-based dishes are widely regarded as a normative practice by a significant portion of the sampled population.

In Polish internet culture and meme creation, Polish people and meme creators actively engage in the creation, sharing, and enhancement of memes, often incorporating political or cultural references. These memes serve the goals of entertaining, expressing dissatisfaction, and sharing humor, and are widely shared on various platforms. The recipients, including internet users and Polish politicians, view, share, and may even become the subject of these memes. The memes frequently feature Polish language, historical, and cultural references, reflecting the creators' desire to express their sentiments in a culturally relevant manner. This behavior is considered a standard and widely accepted practice within the sampled population, indicating that meme creation and sharing are deeply ingrained in Polish internet culture.

In Poland and among Poles, there is a prevalent expression of a strong sense of identity, characterized by stubbornness, pride, and a commitment to preserving cultural purity. This behavior aims to safeguard their cultural identity and shield it from perceived threats. Poles expect others, including themselves and guests, to acknowledge, respect, or respond to their Polish identity. This cultural inclination is influenced by Poland's perceived cultural and racial homogeneity, historical experiences of cultural oppression, and a complex relationship with immigration. The sampled population widely regards the preservation of Polish identity as a normative behavior, reflecting a significant level of acceptance within the cultural group.

In Poland and the Netherlands, Poles and Polish musicians engage in a diverse range of music genres such as rap, hip-hop, folk, pop, and rock, often blending different styles and incorporating cultural elements. Their goal is to entertain, share their cultural heritage, and attract listeners. This musical expression is a significant part of Polish culture and identity, with a strong emphasis on the Polish language and heritage. The sampled population widely regards this musical engagement as a normative and standard practice within the cultural group, reflecting the pervasive influence of music in Polish society and the strong connection to their cultural roots.

In various cities across Poland, both Poles and tourists engage in cultural activities such as exploring the old parts of the city, savoring local cuisine, and socializing in parks. The goal of these activities is to appreciate the city and its attractions. In this host-guest and visitor-city dynamic, the city of Warsaw and tourists reciprocate by providing hospitality and being visited, respectively. This cultural exchange fosters an appreciation for the beautiful views, architecture, and the opportunity for cultural immersion. This behavior is widely regarded as the norm within the sampled population, reflecting a strong consensus on the importance of cultural activities and mutual hospitality in the context of Polish cities.

In public spaces in Poland and abroad, it is common for Poles to avoid unnecessary interactions and maintain personal space when interacting with foreigners and strangers. This behavior is often accompanied by a tendency to express curiosity through staring, as a means to satisfy their interest while keeping a distance. Foreigners and black people are noted to have a low frequency in Poland, which may contribute to the perception of this behavior as extremely unusual by some individuals. Despite this, the sampled population regards this behavior as a standard practice within the cultural group, with a significant portion agreeing that it is a normative way of interacting in public spaces.

In Poland, both Poles and foreigners, particularly in professional settings, engage in language learning, focusing on both Polish and English for practical communication and access to entertainment and culture. This behavior is especially prominent in teacher-student relationships and language learning contexts, where the goal is to communicate effectively and bridge cultural gaps. There is an emphasis on learning Polish in schools and in multicultural professional environments, reflecting the practicality and importance of language skills in these settings. This behavior is widely regarded as common and normative among a significant portion of the sampled population, highlighting the value placed on effective communication and cultural understanding through language learning.

In both urban and rural areas of Poland, people from small towns and cities frequently engage in the practice of migrating between urban centers and the countryside in search of improved opportunities and a more suitable lifestyle. This behavior is driven by the goal of finding better living conditions and career prospects. The cities and countryside reciprocate by receiving these migrants and maintaining a suburban lifestyle. The cultural context is influenced by pre-war inhabitants, stagnation, decay, and cultural shock. This behavior is widely regarded as a common and normative practice within the sampled population, reflecting the prevalent trend of seeking better opportunities and lifestyle through migration between urban and rural areas in Poland.

In various settings such as social gatherings and through platforms like Netflix's foreign language content, Poles are actively engaged in creating, producing, and consuming Polish movies and TV series to uphold their cultural heritage and language. This behavior serves the dual purpose of entertainment and the preservation of Polish culture. Viewers and others reciprocate by watching and learning Polish through these cultural productions. The influence of Norse, Germanic, Slav, French, and English cultures adds depth and diversity to the content. This practice is perceived as moderately normative within the sampled population, indicating that it is neither an unusual behavior nor universally embraced by all members of the cultural group.

In the historical and political contexts surrounding Poland and its people, there is a strong emphasis on striving for independence and sovereignty, especially in the face of historical divisions and external control. The goal is to maintain independence and regain control, reflecting Poland's historical status as a major central European power and the context of partition. This behavior is influenced by the opposition and rule dynamics with other nations and the European Union, who are perceived to either rule or threaten Poland's independence. However, this behavior is not universally accepted within the sampled population, as it is considered controversial and not widely regarded as the standard approach.

In the context of international work and travel, there is a notable pattern of economic and social interactions between Poles, Westerners, Germans, and other countries. Poles are commonly observed working in both Germany and Poland, while Westerners seek job opportunities in Poland. This behavior is driven by the goal of earning a living, promoting positive relations, and seeking employment. In response, Germans and other countries reciprocate by hiring Poles, spending money in Poland, and providing job opportunities. These interactions are influenced by factors such as EU membership, cost of living, and cultural differences. This pattern of cross-border work and economic exchange is regarded as a standard practice by a significant portion of the sampled population, reflecting the interconnectedness and mobility within this international context.

In daily interactions and social life in Poland, Polish people exhibit a blend of friendly, respectful, and occasionally reserved behavior towards individuals ranging from strangers to intimate partners. This behavior includes a tendency to refrain from smiling without a specific reason and engaging in sexual activity without shame. The goal behind these actions is to establish connections, express cultural disaffinity, or simply enjoy socializing. Recipients respond with friendliness, participation in social activities, or by reciprocating a smile. Additionally, Polish people express stereotypes and cultural differences through humor, while placing high value on politeness and respect. This behavior is regarded as relatively normative within the sampled population, indicating that a significant portion of the population finds these actions common and acceptable in Polish social interactions.

In the context of Poland's history and contemporary society, Polish people and the government express strong national pride, fight for freedom, and engage in historical reinterpretation to assert sovereignty, demonstrate solidarity, and rewrite history. This behavior is influenced by Poland's history of struggles, industrial growth, and EU membership. The international community perceives Poland as a victim and acknowledges the influence of Polish judges. This expression of national pride and historical reinterpretation is considered a significant aspect of Polish nationality and politics by a majority of the sampled population.

In various social and professional settings in the UK, Polish people tend to maintain a degree of separation while also striving to assimilate and express emotions, including adopting regional accents. This behavior is driven by the dual goal of preserving their cultural identity while fitting into the new environment. When interacting with Polish people, others, including UK people and local Scottish people, observe and engage with them. Despite having different beliefs, nationalism, and social trust, Polish people in the UK share a similar sense of humor with the local population. This behavior is moderately prevalent within the sampled population, indicating that a significant portion of the group considers it a common approach to integration and cultural preservation.

In Poland, influenced by American press, there has been a noticeable shift in the behavior of Polish people. Initially promoting multiculturalism and tolerance, there has been a transition towards expressing pride in a homogenous white country, opposing the views of social justice warriors (SJWs) and the American press. This shift in opinion is attributed to the perceived negative impact of multiculturalism, leading to a significant division in perspectives. This behavior is considered controversial and highly debated within the sampled population, with approximately half of the population expressing support for this change while the other half continues to advocate for multiculturalism and tolerance.

In Poland, particularly on Christmas Eve and the 6th of December, various gift-givers such as Santa Claus, Starman, and Baby Jesus engage in the tradition of delivering presents to Polish children. The goal of this tradition is to celebrate Christmas and provide gifts to the recipients. On these specific dates, the children eagerly receive the presents, contributing to the festive atmosphere. This gift-giving custom is widely regarded as a normative and integral part of Polish culture, with a unanimous consensus among the sampled population.

In Poland, particularly in Kraków, foreign visitors often request free water in restaurants and may struggle with unfamiliar food options, aiming to quench their thirst and adapt to the local food culture. However, local businesses, as the service providers, typically deny the request for free water and may make efforts to accommodate the preferences of foreign visitors. This behavior is influenced by the fact that foreign visitors are not accustomed to paying for water in restaurants and the lack of widespread international fast food chains in the area. Within this context, the behavior of requesting free water and struggling with unfamiliar food options is considered somewhat unusual or controversial among the sampled population.

In the countryside and rural areas of Poland, residents maintain a distinctive lifestyle characterized by unique speech patterns, clothing, and worldview. This distinctiveness is deeply ingrained within the Polish cultural identity and is widely regarded as the normative way of life by the sampled population. The preservation of these cultural elements reflects a strong sense of tradition and pride among the Polish people, contributing to the richness and diversity of the country's cultural tapestry. This distinctive lifestyle is considered a common and accepted practice among the sampled population, showcasing the strong cultural cohesion and preservation of traditional values within the Polish countryside.

In various settings within Poland, including Polish society and the political climate, it is common for Polish people and society to prioritize the preservation of their cultural identity and uniqueness, while also rejecting the concept of multiculturalism. This behavior is driven by a goal to preserve their cultural identity and assimilate refugees, with a focus on minorities, immigrants, and refugees integrating into Polish culture and receiving care. The society is characterized by a monoethnic composition, patriotism, nationalism, religious beliefs, and ongoing demographic changes. This approach is widely regarded as normative within the sampled population, reflecting a significant consensus on the importance of cultural preservation and assimilation.

In Poland and within Polish literature, it is customary for both Polish people and authors to immerse themselves in the country's culture, including language and literature appreciation, with the goal of learning and enjoying Polish culture. This behavior is reciprocated by Poland and Polish literature, providing a living environment and being highly regarded by the readers. Polish literature is widely considered exceptional, further motivating individuals to engage with and appreciate their cultural heritage. This behavior is regarded as the standard within the sampled population, reflecting a strong cultural norm.

Within the United States, particularly in the Polish diaspora, Polish American individuals and families are known to maintain and adapt their Polish cultural heritage in naming practices. This includes using Polish surnames, English equivalents, and modified versions to align with English spelling and pronunciation rules. The goal behind this behavior is to preserve their cultural identity while assimilating into English-speaking society. Recipients, such as English-speaking society, the military community, and the next generation, generally acknowledge and accept these names, sometimes with mispronunciations or modifications. It is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population, reflecting the strong desire to uphold Polish heritage while navigating life in the United States.

In both Poland and the United States, individuals with Polish ancestry or identity often express their cultural heritage by claiming to be Polish, visiting Poland, and self-identifying as Polish-American. This behavior aims to convey a sense of cultural identity and belonging. The recipients of this expression vary, including immigrants, Polish people, and the author's ancestors, and their responses range from immigration and cultural exchange to acknowledging their Polish roots. There is an emphasis on preserving cultural differences and heritage within this expression of identity. However, this behavior is considered somewhat controversial or less common among the sampled population, indicating that it is not universally embraced or normalized within the Polish-American cultural group.

Polish immigrants and citizens, both in their home country and abroad in locations such as the U.K. and America, actively engage in various activities such as migration, housing, language teaching, and integration efforts. Their primary goal is to seek better opportunities, assimilate, and integrate into the host society. In response, immigrants and Polish society demonstrate acceptance and integration. However, this process is not without its challenges, as individuals may experience culture shock, language barriers, and differences between urban and rural environments. This behavior is widely regarded as normative among the sampled population, reflecting the strong commitment of Polish immigrants and citizens to actively participate in the integration process across different cultural settings.

In Eastern European countries such as Poland, Hungary, and Romania, there is a historical emphasis on preserving cultural identity and maintaining a single race, influenced by religious factors. This behavior is driven by the goal of cultural preservation and diversity, particularly in the context of interactions with Gypsies and other minority groups. The cultural orientation towards the Western world and the historical presence of minorities have also shaped this approach. Within this cultural context, a significant portion of the sampled population regards the focus on cultural preservation and single race as a normative practice, reflecting the value placed on maintaining ethnic and cultural diversity.

In the historical and modern society of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, there is a prevalent practice of tolerating and preserving cultural diversity, with a strong emphasis on mutual respect and unification. The Commonwealth and its people have historically upheld a shared belief in common descent and have actively encouraged the preservation of various cultural identities. This inclusive approach has fostered a history of organic cultural mixing and exchange, leading to the preservation of minority cultures and the expression of diverse cultural identities. The normativity of this behavior is widely regarded as high within the sampled population, reflecting a strong societal norm of cultural preservation and mutual respect. This norm is exemplified through historical events such as the Golden Liberty and the rich literary tradition of 17th-century Polish literature, as well as the resilience against colonization attempts.

In Silesia and Upper Silesia (Opole and Silesian voivodeships), Poland, Silesians and the government actively advocate for autonomy, maintain a distinct regional identity, and work towards preserving the Silesian language and culture. Their goal is to gain recognition for their cultural and linguistic differences and to safeguard the unique Silesian identity. In response, Poland and tourists are expected to acknowledge and record Silesian nationality, as well as show interest in learning about the Silesian culture. The Silesian community has historically been influenced by Austrian and German cultures, and it is important to note that the Silesian language is distinct from Polish. This behavior is widely regarded as normative within the sampled population, reflecting a strong commitment to preserving the Silesian identity and culture.

In Poland, the society actively strives to maintain its cultural identity and traditional norms while simultaneously promoting integration and acceptance, particularly towards immigrants and same-sex couples. The goal is to preserve the rich cultural heritage while fostering inclusivity within the community. Immigrants and same-sex couples, in turn, seek to adopt Polish culture and advocate for marriage and adoption rights. Historically known for tolerance, recent laws reflect a shift towards more traditional marriage norms. This behavior is widely regarded as normative within the sampled population, indicating a strong societal emphasis on preserving cultural traditions while also embracing integration and acceptance.

In both urban and rural areas, including small towns and the outskirts of Warsaw, LGBTQ+ individuals and their families cautiously express their identity and affection, aiming to avoid discrimination and violence. This behavior is influenced by the fear of negative consequences and the prevalent experience of homophobia, including verbal and physical abuse, from society and the police. The government's rhetoric further contributes to the widespread homophobia, leading LGBTQ+ individuals to refrain from openly expressing their identity to evade adverse reactions. This cautious approach to expressing identity is considered an unusual behavior within the sampled population, reflecting the challenging and discriminatory environment faced by LGBTQ+ individuals in Poland.

In Poland and among Polish communities, it is common for people to engage in various social and linguistic practices, such as speaking for oneself, sharing opinions, using colloquialisms, and expressing emotions openly. This cultural behavior reflects a strong emphasis on individual expression and communication within the community. The sampled population widely regards these practices as normative, indicating that a significant portion of the population finds these behaviors to be commonplace and acceptable within the Polish cultural context.

In Poland and within Polish cuisine, it is customary for both locals and Polish people to consume a diverse array of traditional foods, such as potatoes, pickle soup, bread, and sausage, often considering them as staple items or for their health benefits. When hosting visitors, it is common for the hosts to offer these traditional dishes, encouraging their guests to try Polish food. This practice is widely regarded as a normative behavior within the sampled population, with a significant portion agreeing that consuming traditional Polish foods is a standard and expected part of the cultural experience.

In Poland, when consuming pizza, it is customary for people to prefer garlic sauce as a normal addition or side. This cultural preference is widely regarded as a common practice among the sampled population. Additionally, the Polish are also known for their daily consumption of potatoes. The inclusion of garlic sauce with pizza is considered a normative behavior within the Polish cultural context, with a significant portion of the sampled population agreeing that it is a standard practice.

In Poland, especially during the summer, people are accustomed to experiencing and adapting to a wide range of weather conditions, including cold winters and hot summers. The perception of Poland's climate as predominantly cold is contrasted by occasional heatwaves that can reach up to 40 degrees Celsius. Despite this, the population is known for their adaptability and resilience in the face of such varying weather patterns. This behavior is widely regarded as a normative aspect of the culture, with a significant portion of the sampled population acknowledging and embracing the need to adjust to these diverse climatic conditions.

In the context of Polish food culture, it is common for people to consume a variety of sausages, including blood sausage and hotdogs. These sausages are integral to Polish cuisine and are enjoyed in various dishes. The blood sausage, similar to black pudding, holds a significant place in Polish culinary traditions. It is worth noting that commercial sausages in the USA may contain unexpected ingredients, highlighting the contrast between traditional Polish sausages and those found in other regions. This practice of consuming different types of sausages is widely regarded as a normative behavior within the sampled population, reflecting its strong cultural significance in Polish food culture.

In Poland and within Polish cuisine, it is customary for people to actively participate in the traditional preparation, consumption, and promotion of pierogi, which holds a significant place as a staple and symbol of Polish culinary heritage. Pierogi, a type of filled dumpling, is deeply ingrained in Polish culture and is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population. The act of engaging with pierogi aligns with the cultural pride and appreciation for traditional culinary practices, reflecting the strong influence of food in Polish identity and daily life.

In the context of Poland and its people, there is a prevalent experience of a rich and intricate history, characterized by resilience, survival, and a profound sense of immortality. This historical narrative, spanning from the 700s to the present, is often considered underrated and encompasses a wide array of significant events. The sampled population widely regards this resilience and sense of immortality as a normative aspect of Polish culture, reflecting the majority's acknowledgment of the enduring and survivalist nature of the Polish people throughout history.

In Poland and within Polish culture, it is common for people to engage in alcohol consumption, particularly vodka and beer, often starting at a young age and with a reputation for heavy drinking. The legal drinking age of 18, with variations in drinking habits and alcohol content, contributes to the prevalence of this behavior. This pattern of alcohol consumption is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population.

In Poland, during social interactions, people, including tourists and travelers, engage in various forms of hospitality such as visiting, inviting others for tea, and requesting invitations. The goal of these actions is to demonstrate hospitality, socialize, and allow individuals to experience the culture of Poland. In return, guests and other individuals are expected to accept invitations and participate in social activities. Poland is perceived as underrated, and visitors may feel like celebrities due to the warm reception they receive. This behavior is widely regarded as a standard practice within the sampled population, indicating that a significant portion of individuals in the cultural group consider it a common and expected part of social interactions in Poland.

In Poland, it is common for people to express admiration for the country's beauty, loyalty, and natural wonders, often drawing comparisons to the beauty of Spain. This admiration reflects a deep appreciation for Poland's cultural and natural heritage, with a particular emphasis on its aesthetic appeal and the loyalty of its people. The act of comparing Poland to Spain in terms of beauty is widely regarded as a normative behavior within the sampled population. This comparison serves as a testament to the high esteem in which Poland's attributes are held, showcasing a strong sense of national pride and appreciation for the country's unique qualities.

In Poland and Polish communities, it is common for people to enjoy a wide variety of sweets and snacks, including unique flavors and traditional treats like krówki. This appreciation for a diverse range of confectionery is deeply ingrained in the culture and is widely regarded as a normative behavior by the sampled population. The love for sweets and snacks reflects the cultural significance of indulging in traditional and innovative flavors, showcasing a strong connection to culinary heritage and a shared enjoyment of these treats within the community.

In Poland and Polish communities abroad, both locals and tourists commonly engage in shopping for Polish products, such as food, souvenirs, and other goods, often finding them to be of good quality and reasonably priced. These products have a notable presence in supermarkets and specialty stores, and are generally considered to be high quality and affordable. This behavior is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population, reflecting a strong preference for and confidence in Polish-made goods.

In Polish daily meals and special occasions, it is customary for people to emphatically consume potatoes in various forms. This includes cooking them in different ways, eating them with vinegar, and using them in multiple dishes. Potatoes hold a significant presence in Polish cuisine, reflecting their cultural significance and versatility in culinary practices. This behavior of consuming potatoes is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population, indicating a high level of acceptance and prevalence.

In Poland and within Polish cuisine, it is common for people to enjoy a wide range of traditional dishes such as kaszanka, karpatka, and kiszka, which often contain unique ingredients like blood and onions. Kaszanka, in particular, is a traditional Polish dish made of pig's blood, showcasing the cultural preference for utilizing unconventional ingredients in their cuisine. This culinary practice is widely regarded as normative within the sampled population, with a significant portion of individuals embracing and celebrating the consumption of these traditional dishes.

In Poland, it is common for people to use unique and specific toilets, which may include a poop shelf, and to actively participate in waste recycling. The toilets are typically labeled for men and women, and there are usually five separate recycle bins for different materials, reflecting a strong emphasis on environmental consciousness and sustainability. This behavior is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population, indicating a high level of acceptance and prevalence.

In Poland, it is common for people to dress fashionably, often leaning towards overdressing or donning traditional clothing while prioritizing both comfort and style. This sartorial preference is widely regarded as the norm within the sampled population, reflecting a strong emphasis on personal presentation and a celebration of cultural attire. The act of dressing fashionably is deeply ingrained in the societal fabric and is considered a standard practice among a significant portion of the sampled population.

It’s considered rude to not be on time. ‘To be on time’ means if you arrange meeting at 4.00 pm you will arrive exactly at this time, especially if it’s a business meeting, lecture, appointment etc. In social situations, like meeting friends, being 5-10 minutes late is acceptable. S ervices like trains, buses, etc . tend to run on time . P unctuality is valued and most people tend to cove t their time.
Women hold the same professions as m en in most all arenas. There are many who still take to the traditional homemaker role, but opportunities are open and available for all.

The t humb s up sign means o.k. or good, and the “okay’ sign is recognized as well. It’s considered rude to point with a finger, it’s best to use the whole hand. Putting your thumb in between the middle and index fingers while making a thumb, means “you’ll get zip” or “nothing/zero”.

Giving someone the ‘middle finger’ is a rude gesture. S tanding close to somebody that hasn’t finished their meal in a restaurant is considered rude. Standing with your hands in your pockets during conversation is looked down upon. B urping while eating; jaywalking ; drinking in the street or public places; and smoking in non-designated areas, are all usually considered rude.

The drinking age and smoking age is 1 8 years old somewhat enforced, Penalties for possession, use, or trafficking in illegal drugs are severe, and convicted offenders can expect long jail sentences and heavy fines.

For Men - a conservative yet stylish suit is acceptable. Darker colors tend to be the norm. B lack shoes and belt, no tie pin, and accessories should be limited to a watch and/or wedding ring. For W omen : stylish yet classic business suits or dresses/pants and blouses in corporate settings. Avoid wearing overly expensive and/or elaborate accessories. Closed toe shoes are most appropriate. Business casual and other less formal attire may be appropriate in certain industries.

It’s best to use a person's title and their surname until invited to use their first name. Pan is for Mr . , Pani for Mrs. and Miss . There is no specific protocol surrounding the giving and receiving of business cards. It is always best to treat the card with respect.

Business meetings tend to begin and end with a bit of small talk. It is best to wait for the host to begin and end the business talk. Being humble is valued so avoid boasting or making claims that may be misinterpreted as arrogance.
Decisions tend to be made from the top down.

Simple gifts such as souvenirs from one’s country or company may be appropriate for initial business meetings, but are not expected. If invited to a Polish home, it is appropriate to bring good quality wine /spirits, chocolates/sweets or something simple from your home country. When it comes to gifts, it’s best to avoid anything overly expensive or elaborate.

Most universities start in October and end in July with 3 month vacation in between. Generally all kind of dress are acceptable for students. However, for women very provocative (short skirt, deep neckline) clothing would be perceived as impolite and improper. Teaching methods depend on the course. Lectures are very common and group work is as well. Grades at the university level use a numeric system from 2 to 5, with 5 being the highest and 3 the pass/fail level. Grades are given in increment of 0.5.

Students socialize by going to pubs, and discos but the majority meet at parties in student houses or dorms. Drinking and smoking is acceptable for both men and women. Poles tend to drink a lot. Women don't tend to be very forward. Men usually ask women out on dates.

Students tend to be very stylish and well dressed. Casual clothing such as flip flops and Ugg boots are considered tacky. Each student wants to stand out and both girls and boys won't buy an article of clothing if their friend has it.
